sections.skill: Value employee benefits and compare job offers by total compensation

questions.prompt: Which item is an employee BENEFIT rather than wages?

choices.text: Overtime pay at time and a half
A commission on each sale the worker makes
Hourly pay for a Saturday shift

questions.intro: Total compensation is everything an employer provides for your work: wages or salary plus benefits. Common benefits include health insurance (the employer often pays part of the cost), retirement plans with matching contributions, paid time off, and sometimes tuition help or transit passes.
questions.feedback: Employer-paid health insurance is a benefit; the other three are forms of pay.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Zoe earns $50,000. Her employer matches 50% of her 401(k) contributions, up to 6% of salary. Zoe contributes 6% ($3,000). How much does the employer add?
questions.intro: Many employers match retirement contributions, for example "50% of what you contribute, up to 6% of pay." The match is extra money for your retirement, but you only receive it if you contribute.
questions.feedback: Zoe contributes $3,000; the employer adds 50% of that: $1,500.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers

misconceptions.D: Gives the total of both contributions

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Zoe's coworker earns $50,000 under the same match (50% of contributions, up to 6% of salary) but contributes only 2% ($1,000). How much potential match does the coworker give up each year?
questions.feedback: Full match possible: 50% × $3,000 = $1,500. Match received: 50% × $1,000 = $500. Missed: $1,000.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers

misconceptions.A: Gives the match received instead of the match missed

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Offer A: $48,000 salary; the employee pays $100 per month for health insurance. Offer B: $50,000; the employee pays $250 per month for the same coverage. After subtracting health premiums, which pays more per year, and by how much?
questions.intro: To compare offers fairly, subtract the costs you would pay (such as your share of health premiums) and add the value of benefits you would receive (such as a retirement match).
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A job gives 10 paid vacation days. Lin earns $200 per day. What is the dollar value of that paid time off?
questions.feedback: Paid time off is pay for days not worked: 10 × $200 = $2,000.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers

misconceptions.D: Thinks paid time off has no value

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.relationship: Comparing offers requires seeing benefits as part of what a job pays.

questions.prompt: What does "total compensation" include?

choices.text: Only the hourly wage or salary
Only the take-home pay after taxes
Only bonuses earned at year end
Pay plus the value of benefits

questions.correct_answer: Pay plus the value of benefits
questions.intro: Compensation is everything you receive for work. Wages are the pay; benefits are the extras, such as health insurance, retirement contributions, and paid time off, which have real dollar value.
questions.feedback: Total compensation = pay + benefits.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which choice is paid time off (PTO)?

choices.text: A lunch break you are not paid for

questions.intro: Paid time off means days you are paid for even though you do not work, such as vacation, sick days, or holidays.
questions.feedback: Paid vacation days are paid time off.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: An employer pays $400 per month toward an employee's health insurance. What is that worth per year?
questions.feedback: $400 × 12 = $4,800 of value per year.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: What is a 401(k)?

choices.text: A type of bank checking account for paying monthly bills
A form used to apply for a job
A retirement savings plan offered through an employer

questions.correct_answer: A retirement savings plan offered through an employer
questions.intro: A 401(k) is a retirement savings plan offered by many private employers. Workers contribute part of each paycheck, often with tax benefits, and some employers add a match. (Public schools and many nonprofits offer a similar 403(b).)
questions.feedback: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement savings plan.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Two jobs pay the same salary. Job X pays the entire premium for health coverage. Job Y offers none, so the worker must buy the same coverage for $300 a month. How much more does Job Y effectively cost the worker per year?
questions.feedback: $300 × 12 = $3,600 a year that Job X's benefit covers.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers

misconceptions.A: Ignores the cost of buying coverage

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: Find a percent of a quantity
sections.relationship: Employer match and contribution rates are percents of salary.

ref_skill.name: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100

sections.relationship: Comparing offers combines monthly and yearly amounts and percents.

questions.prompt:
Offer C: $52,000 salary, no retirement match, employee health premium $150 per month.
Offer D: $50,000 salary, 401(k) match worth $2,000 per year if you contribute, employee health premium $100 per month.
If you contribute enough to get the full match, which offer is worth more per year, and by how much?
questions.intro: A fair comparison adds the value of benefits you will actually use and subtracts costs you will actually pay. A match counts only if you contribute enough to earn it.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers

misconceptions.D: Adds the premium difference the wrong way

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A 401(k) match "vests" over 3 years. Ali leaves after 1 year. What does vesting mean for him?

choices.text: He may forfeit the unvested part of the employer's match
He loses his own contributions as well as the match
He keeps everything because matches always vest at once

questions.correct_answer: He may forfeit the unvested part of the employer's match
questions.intro: Vesting is ownership over time. Your own 401(k) contributions are always yours. An employer's contributions may vest gradually, and if you leave before you are fully vested, you can lose the unvested part.
questions.feedback: Unvested employer money can be forfeited; employee contributions are always 100% vested.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers

misconceptions.B: Thinks his own money can be forfeited

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Under a plan where the match vests 20% per year of service, how much of a $1,500 match has Ali earned after 1 year?
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers

misconceptions.A: Assumes nothing vests in year one

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which benefit is easiest to overlook when comparing jobs?
questions.feedback: Benefits such as tuition help can be worth thousands of dollars if you will use them.

questions.prompt: Which source is MOST reliable for typical pay and benefits in an occupation?

choices.text: Government labor data and job postings
A single viral social media post about a high salary
An advertisement for a training course

questions.correct_answer: Government labor data and job postings
questions.intro: Researching typical income and benefits before choosing a career or job helps you negotiate and plan. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes pay data and job outlooks by occupation; job postings show current offers.
questions.feedback: Official labor statistics and actual postings give the most reliable picture.

sections.skill: The hidden costs of a job

questions.prompt: Job E pays $20 per hour, 40 hours a week. The commute costs $12 per day for 5 days. What is the weekly pay after commuting costs?
questions.intro: A job's real value can depend on costs it creates: commuting (fuel, parking, transit), uniforms, tools, or child care. Subtracting them gives a clearer comparison.
questions.feedback: Pay: $800. Commute: 5 × $12 = $60. After commuting: $740.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Job E pays $740 a week after $60 of commuting costs, for 40 hours of work. The commute also takes 1 unpaid hour each day, 5 days a week. Counting commute time, what are the weekly earnings after commuting costs per hour of time spent (work + commute)?
questions.feedback: Time: 40 + 5 = 45 hours. Earnings after costs: $740. $740 ÷ 45 ≈ $16.44 per hour.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Job E pays $20 per hour, but commuting costs $12 a day for 5 days. Job F pays $19 per hour, fully remote, with no commuting costs. Which earns more per week for 40 hours of work, after commuting costs?
questions.feedback: Job F: 40 × $19 = $760 with no costs, which beats Job E's $740 after commuting by $20.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which cost should be subtracted when comparing two jobs?

choices.text: Required uniforms the worker must buy
Groceries the worker would buy anyway
Rent the worker pays either way
A phone bill the worker pays either way

questions.correct_answer: Required uniforms the worker must buy
questions.feedback: Subtract costs the job causes, not costs you would have anyway.
questions.topic: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.
